title: Ask HN: Dark mode for HN please? (2026)
summary:
The 2020 thread does a lot: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23197966

It shows 100 solutions in light of Parkinson’s Law of Triviality. Intense opinions and discussion.

It teaches about alligator energy and how they can live without food for up to two years.

It teaches that this site should look like top, yet I’ve rarely seen top on a white terminal in the past two decades. This does exist, nofi.

Workarounds exist, and those are “mid” janky shit shows. One I tried was an iOS app. It flashes the page between light and dark on every click. Aside from not being a solution, it’s nausea-inducing, takes 20+ steps to install, requires you to blindly trust the app without a Git repo, and requires you to change your OS. It shows that running 20 miles to solve this is what people do to get to any promise of a solution. So many of these exist that it’s just a swamp of well intended nightmares making the problem worse.

HN is filled with love for fonts, styling, terminal themes, CSS madness, and quirks. Yet here I am with empty hands and little karma, with a screen that burns into my eyes at night. The last bastion of light, in more ways than intended.

As with the resolution to PHP’s sleep(), going with something that keeps things running unchanged for those who don’t move, but tailoring it further for those who want it, I’d opt for two extremes for logged-in users:

A: Adding a custom CSS styling text area, allowing for maximized creativity, experimentation, hacking, and freedom, and supporting any matter of taste and necessity. It is just fun, and this might be shut down due to arguments about security, bloat, resetting mistakes, and such. But it’s still the most fun and expressive option.

B: Having a drop-down setting for some styles, where just inverting the whole site with two lines of CSS using `filter: invert()` works for me, or choosing whatever theme is agreed upon somewhere. We have millions of dollars’ worth of CSS talent on this site and similar amounts of LLM investment to get something tasteful, respectful, well thought out, and just great. Make it a contest. Hurt me plenty.

This is not a dilemma, but I hope to inspire a move toward a native solution so I can read HN at night without the abracadabra of altering my OS, browser, trust, or, well, anything outside this site.

I’m also fine with no solution to this if the answer is: You should not read HN at night for a better and healthier life. Then add that to HN policy. I didn’t find that.

Sorry for bringing this up again.

title: Ask HN: What have you built privately with AI that you'd like to share?
summary:
An idea has circulated that a lot of us are just privately building software for our own projects without sharing the build

We could however share the ideas of what we're building so that other people could build sometime similar to fill their own needs or the ideas could be incorporated in to other projects

A lot of random things come to mind for me, like I started (but for now abandoned) some kind of picture icon viewer by date on Linux desktop. A lot of smartphone file viewers display pics this way automatically and it lets you look at what pics you've accumulated day by day, but I didn't see this feature on different Linux file viewers (and it was apparently a requested feature others were looking for).

So what have you built privately with AI that you might like to share ideas about?

title: Addressing EU Cyber Resilience Act
summary:
By Jacob Mammoliti, Solutions Architect, RapidFort The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is a regulation (EU 2024/2847) that defines mandatory cybersecurity requirements for all products with digital elements sold in EU markets. Reporting obligations began on Sept. 11, with full enforcement commencing on Dec. 11, 2027. The CRA sets new requirements for teams working with containers and Kubernetes that impact how cloud native applications are built, distributed, and maintained throughout their lifecycle. Cloud Native Environments and CRA Scope Regardless of where a distributing organization is located, the CRA covers all container images, Kubernetes operators, and Helm charts with commercial support that are available to EU customers. The regulation specifies its scope as “products with digital elements” available in EU markets, and that also includes a lot of the cloud native stack. CRA scope covers container images distributed publicly, commercial Kubernetes operators, open source with commercial backing, and Helm charts with commercial support. Open-source projects may also be impacted, including those with commercial backing or support contracts. In addition, the regulation requires a compliance chain throughout the cloud native supply chain. CRA Requirements for Container Teams The CRA introduces requirements that directly impact how teams build and operate container infrastructure. These categories include: Vulnerability Management – SBOM data, continuous monitoring, and 24-hour ENISA reporting for exploited vulnerabilities. Security by Design and Default – Hardened base images, minimal attack surfaces, and secure defaults as regulatory requirements. Long-Term Security (5+ Years) – Ongoing security updates, rebuild pipelines, and backward-compatible patching for product lifetime. This Act specifies that base images must be hardened with unnecessary components eliminated and secure configurations applied before products are made available on the market. The regulation orders what many in the cloud native community have long wanted – now minimal attack surfaces and secure defaults are regulatory requirements rather than recommendations. As a result of the CRA, organizations must maintain Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) data, continuously monitor for vulnerabilities, and remediate within defined timeframes. Under the Act’s Article 14, actively exploited vulnerabilities must result in an early warning to The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (maintaining the acronym from the agency’s previous name European Network and Information Security Agency – ENISA) within 24 hours of discovery, followed by a full notification within 72 hours. This mandates that organizations’ detection and incident response processes need to operate at scale across clusters. Now products require security updates for a minimum of five years from the date of being available on the market, or throughout the expected product lifetime if that period is shorter, as stated in Article 13 of the CRA. For container teams, this requires tracking container versions deployed in customer environments, ensuring backward compatibility, and maintaining rebuild pipelines for older images – all while addressing security issues discovered years after release.

title: What is still hard to become good at as AI makes coding easier?
summary:
Since LLMs came, how I build software changed for so many reasons. Since then, I’ve spent most of my time deciding what I want to build, how I want to build it, how I want to give the context, checking the result, seeing if there is an error, and paving the way for the LLM to do the right thing. And the difficult part, which is writing code and getting everything right, is handled by the LLM surprisingly well, from my work and the people around me and people who I look up to on the internet.

Until now, my edge was that you can get really far by understanding how computers work, like networking and CLI, kernels, reading errors, and following documents. You can get very far. But that strong edge is now fading because of how good LLMs are becoming lately. It won’t take that long. That edge would be gone when LLMs get much better at switching to the specific context of things. They still can do it, but you need to pave the way for them.

Now, people are saying you should have better judgment of what to develop for the future. But the issue is that I haven’t identified a hard thing worth committing to since LLMs came along.

I’m in my early career and trying to decide where I should invest my serious efforts. What capabilities remain difficult to acquire, are very niche, and aren’t something lots of people want to work on? There has to be something where human expertise remains valuable, including work where a human is still much cheaper than using LLMs.

I’m not looking for an answer like, “XYZ types of sites are very hard to build, and you should build one yourself and make money.” What I’m missing is a concrete problem, who needs it solved, what makes it difficult, and a path into working on it.

I’m not looking for an easy answer. I’m trying to see what you and other people have run into or understand about what’s going on right now. I need to find a hard thing to do, and I haven’t found one I feel confident committing to. Can you help me find one?

title: Tell HN: Getting spam after commenting on monthly Who's Hiring posts. Who else?
summary:
I made a post on the monthly Who's Hiring thread, and since then I've been inundated by spammy AI slop messages of people pitching their vibe coded job search platforms. It's junk mail to the point that I probably won't post on a Who's Hiring thread again. I'm looking for real opportunities, not to sign up for yet another person's dead end job search platform. I'm just curious if other HN folks have had the same experience recently?

Here's the email I just got today:

> I'm Kelvin — I run Loker Dollar, a small job board for remote roles that pay in USD. I came across your post on Hacker News's “Who wants to be hired?” thread — the React Native, React + JavaScript one, based in Nomadic. US and EU, and it's exactly the kind of profile the companies we work with are hiring for.

> Being upfront about what I did: I added an anonymized version of your post to our recruiter search so hiring teams can find you. Your name and email stay hidden — nobody sees them unless you say yes.

> Two one-click choices, no account needed:

> Claim & manage my profile

> Decide how you appear and who can reach you.

> Remove me

> Delete the listing, and I'll never email you again.

I'm not sure what, if anything, can be done to prevent people scraping and spamming these threads, but I do feel that these threads are being abused, and I really wish there were a way to only allow people who have verified opportunities to contact me about their own opportunities.

title: Ask HN: Beyond traces, how do you know your agent did the job?
summary:
I keep going back and forth on this.

Traces and logs tell me what the agent did: every tool call, retry, token, and step.

That's useful when something breaks. What I'm less sure about is whether that tells me the agent actually did the right thing.

A run can look clean and still miss what I wanted. Or it can "finish" without the outcome really being done. So finished and succeeded aren't the same thing.

I haven't made up my mind how to check for that, but I'm experimenting a lot with extracting intents from my agent and correlating among them.

Curious how you do it:

- Do you capture intent and outcome explicitly (e.g. giving a tool to the agent to "declare" it), or infer them after the fact from the traces?

- What kind of "questions" do you "ask" your traces?
